A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mobility-based multimodal representation work, renamed from MobCLIP to MoRA. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original downstream prediction results, scaling experiments, ablations, sampling and grid-resolution analyses, and distillation results.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, anchor-choice and neighborhood-graph comparisons, and auxiliary-modality ablations.

M1.justification: The LINE-initialized LightGCN, auxiliary encoders, contrastive objective and MLP distillation remain unchanged; the new 'asymmetric' terminology does not change the loss. v4 additionally evaluates and recommends a variant replacing mobility edges with direct cell-neighborhood edges (Sections 4.4–5).

E1.justification: v4 removes elevation and forest-coverage evaluation, narrowing the benchmark from 11 social, economic and natural tasks to nine social and economic tasks. Their distillation results and natural-domain ablation/sampling results are also removed. The pretraining modalities and Chinese geographical coverage are retained; Jiangsu was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v4 adds AlphaEarth to the nationwide comparison in Table 2 while retaining the six original baselines. New Table 3 evaluates HREP, ReCP and ReFound against MoRA in Jiangsu. These three methods were cited but not evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 revises demographic preprocessing from five-year age bands and gender to ten-year bands, gender and work-home status. Point-level evaluation changes from assigning grid embeddings to individual points to aggregating point values within grids. Added comparisons specify AlphaEarth pixel pooling and Jiangsu baseline training/inference procedures. The main split, training budget and prediction models remain unchanged; the revised descriptions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds comparisons of mobility, demographic, POI and image anchors; a mobility-versus-neighborhood graph control; and individual auxiliary-modality removals (Figure 3 and Table 6). These directly test the backbone and fusion choices beyond v1's component removals. Existing scaling, graph-sampling and grid-resolution studies are retained, while natural-domain ablation results disappear.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten repeated downstream runs and report means with standard deviations in Table 2. Neither introduces a different uncertainty-estimation practice, explicit seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Additional tables report point estimates, as supplementary tables already did in v1.

E6.justification: The nine retained proposed-model scores in Table 2 are unchanged, but new comparator results alter rankings: AlphaEarth scores 0.63 on nighttime lights versus MoRA's 0.62. v4 adds Jiangsu comparison and modality-ablation results and removes natural-task results. Scaling, grid-resolution and retained distillation numbers match v1. The headline 35% versus 12.9% advantages concern different task/comparator sets, not a same-setting performance decline.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the distillation objective retain the same mathematics. v4's LLM and spatial-syntax analogy supplies conceptual motivation, without adding formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations.

C1.justification: v1 presents the first nationwide general-purpose encoder spanning human and natural domains, with an approximately 35% advantage. v4 instead emphasizes human-centric functional representations, nine socio-economic tasks and a 12.9% advantage. It also newly claims, with qualification, the first empirical evidence of geospatial scaling laws, although the scaling experiment is retained.

C2.justification: v4 develops the interpretation of mobility as spatial syntax, explains the new anchor and graph controls, recommends a neighborhood-based alternative, and discusses geographically sparse task coverage. Appendix A.6 corrects the resolution interpretation: finer grids generally help, with crime as the exception, replacing v1's opposite generalization with population as the exception. The underlying resolution table is unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 adds downstream sample counts, discloses five-year crime aggregation followed by log(1 + count), and describes baseline adaptation and training/inference choices. Code-access directions change from a placeholder/anonymized address to the named MoRA GitHub repository. Core hardware, optimizer, training-time and distillation specifications remain unchanged; actual online availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially reposition the paper around physical Earth-observation representations versus human-centric functional representations. v4 introduces AlphaEarth and citations to Brown et al., Cole et al. and Mac Aodha et al., and expands discussion of regional methods and PDFM. HREP, ReCP and ReFound are newly evaluated, rather than newly cited.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and discussion are extensively rewritten around human-centric representation learning. The paper is renamed, the distillation discussion moves into evaluation, and appendices are reorganized. Dedicated ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements replace the NeurIPS checklist.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redesigned from two panels to three, adding anchor comparisons and the neighborhood variant while dropping natural-task groups. v4 adds dataset-distribution maps and two tables, adds sample counts to Table 1, and removes natural-task and average columns from Table 2. Existing appendix tables are relocated and renumbered within the ICLR layout.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens support for the central mobility-backbone claim by addressing v1's reliance on coordinate/image comparators and limited mechanism controls. Relevant regional baselines and direct anchor, neighborhood and modality tests make that claim more assessable; the narrower scope and corrected resolution interpretation also improve alignment with evidence. Removing natural-task results reduces documented breadth, and prose still overstates wins contradicted by Tables 3 and 6. These shortcomings temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in empirical support.
